title: The Transactional Layer of Local Government Is About to Disappear
excerpt: The Thesis Much of the daily work of local government involves transferring information from one ...
content:
## The Thesis



Much of the daily work of local government involves transferring information from one location to another. This includes processing permits, licenses, applications, inspections, and renewals. Each of these tasks consists of completing forms, making routing decisions, and filing documents. When you consider this work over the course of a year, it adds up to thousands of hours of staff time spent on tasks that do not require human judgment.

That work is going to disappear. Not because government got faster. Because the tools finally caught up.


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


The Microsoft 365 license your municipality currently holds includes Power Automate, SharePoint, and Power Apps; there's no need for additional purchases. The challenging aspect isn't acquiring the tools; it's effectively integrating them to create a complete solution for your workflow.


## The build


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


The Village of Lincolnshire needed a better way to handle non-police employment applications. Old process: PDF download, email it in, someone re-keys the data, attachments live in inboxes.

New process: one Survey123 form, one Power Automate flow, one SharePoint hub. When an applicant hits submit:

- Form data lands in a structured SharePoint list, validated
- A branded Word document is auto-generated across eight sections
- Every attachment files itself in the document library
- HR gets the full packet by email


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


Submit to HR inbox: under 30 seconds.

## What HR sees


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



The HR view is a card-based hub, every application color-coded by pipeline stage, with fit score, eligibility flags, and direct links to the resume. Click any card and a custom-formatted review form opens. No tabs to flip. No folders to dig through.


## The five-year picture


This is one process. There are dozens like it in every municipality: business licenses, permits, inspections, FOIA requests, code complaints, and volunteer applications. They all follow the same pattern: structured intake, automated document generation, file routing, and notification.

Once you've built one, the next takes a fraction of the time.

The municipalities that figure this out early will spend their staff time on judgment, policy, and resident relationships. The ones that don't will spend the next decade re-keying applications into spreadsheets, and paying premium rates to consulting firms for work that should be in-house competence by then.


## Where to start

If you're in local government and reading this, your IT or innovation team probably already has the licenses. Find one process that's currently painful, one that involves a form, an email, and someone re-keying data. Build that one first. The next ones are easier.

title: How We Replaced Email Approvals With Power Apps
excerpt: The Problem A department submits a check request.
content:
## The Problem


A department submits a check request. They send an email.

It sits.

Someone follows up. The approver is out of office. A reminder goes to the wrong person. A week passes.

For the Village of Glencoe, this was every week. Early check requests were routing through email with no visibility, no structure, and no audit trail. Finance was spending 3–4 hours every week just chasing down approvals.

That's the problem we fixed.


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## What We Built


One connected solution on Microsoft 365.

- Microsoft Forms - structured intake with invoice upload
- Power Apps - approval dashboard and mobile interface
- Power Automate - automated routing, reminders, audit trail
- SharePoint - document library and intranet SOP

No new software. No new licenses. Everything already in their environment.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)
**


## The App

The Overview dashboard is the command center.

Finance opens the app and sees every request in flight, total, pending, with Finance, rejected, and paid. Real-time. No inbox. No spreadsheet.



Each request card shows the payee, amount, department, and a status badge. Below is a stage tracker showing exactly where it sits across all four approval stages.
Click into any request, and you get the full picture. Requester info, payment details, business justification, comments, the approval trail, and all attachments in one panel.


## The Crown Jewel

The Approval Trail.

Every approver. Every timestamp. Built automatically on every single request.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)




Approver out of office? Edit the trail, reassign to a delegate in seconds. The workflow never stops.

And the whole app works on mobile. Executives can approve from anywhere.


## The Automation

Three Power Automate flows run everything behind the scenes.

Submission Flow - fires the moment the form is submitted. Routes to SharePoint. Notifies approvers. No human handoff.

Weekly Reminder Flow - every Wednesday at 9 AM, a personalized reminder goes to every approver with pending items. Nobody gets a generic blast.

Audit Trail Flow - when a request completes, it auto-generates the audit document and attaches it to the SharePoint record. Filed automatically.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## The Results

Approval Cycle - 5–7 days → Under 2 days

Manual Coordination - 3–4 hrs/week → Under 1 hr/week

Audit Trail - None → Every request, automatically

Mobile Approvals - Not possible → Any device, anywhere

Estimated $7,000–$10,000 in annual value. Built in three months.



## The Core Takeaway


The technology wasn't the hard part.

Understanding the process well enough to design something that actually fits how the team works was the work. Discovery, iteration, and real UAT with the Finance team made the difference.

The result is a system that runs itself.

That's what replacing email approvals actually looks like.

title: JavaScript AI Build-a-thon Hack Building CivicLens: A Multi-Agent AI Platform
excerpt: How I built an agentic AI system that helps residents report potholes, predict infrastructure fai...
content:
*How I built an agentic AI system that helps residents report potholes, predict infrastructure failures, and hold local government accountable, using JavaScript, GitHub Models, and the Model Context Protocol.*

## Try It

- **Live Demo**: [civiclens-app.azurewebsites.net](https://civiclens-app.azurewebsites.net)
- **GitHub**: [github.com/JonEricEubanks/CivicLens](https://github.com/JonEricEubanks/CivicLens)


---

## The Problem

Every city maintains databases of potholes, broken sidewalks, and work orders. But this data is locked behind FOIA requests, 311 phone trees, and PDF reports nobody reads.

We work with local government and when they request residents or Board members "are there any potholes near the school?" the answer required calling public works, waiting on hold, and hoping someone could cross-reference repair logs with school locations. That's a question a machine should answer in seconds.

**CivicLens** is my answer: an AI agent that turns municipal infrastructure data into plain-language intelligence, lets residents file service requests on a map, and uses a Weibull survival model to help staff predict which repairs are most likely to fail next.

---

## Architecture: A 5-Stage Multi-Agent Pipeline



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


```
Intent Classification (4-model vote) → ReAct Data Agent → Quality Feedback → RAG Synthesis → Report Formatting
```

**Stage 1 — Intent Classification:** GPT-4o-mini classifies queries into 12 intent classes and extracts structured filters. But here's the twist: **four classifiers vote in parallel** GPT-4o-mini, Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, a keyword baseline, and an **on-device MobileBERT model** running via ONNX Runtime (`@huggingface/transformers`). If 3 of 4 agree, consensus overrides the primary. The local ONNX model means CivicLens classifies intents even when all cloud APIs are down. A sliding-window conversation memory (10 turns, persisted to disk) handles follow-ups like "*what about sidewalks?*" without repeating context.

**Stage 2 — ReAct Data Agent:** An LLM-driven **Reason + Act loop** that selects from 16 MCP tools, calls them in parallel, reflects on results, and iterates up to 5 times. Tool results are cached (5-min TTL). Falls back to deterministic routing if the LLM is unavailable.

**Stage 3 — RAG-Grounded Synthesis:** Reports are grounded in an **11-document knowledge base** (municipal codes, APWA repair standards, school zone safety, weather data, budget frameworks). Retrieval uses dense embeddings with a TF-IDF fallback using domain-boosted keywords. Inline citations `[1], [2]` reference specific source documents.

**Quality Feedback Loop:** If data coverage drops below 40%, the pipeline automatically retries with broadened filters before synthesis begins.

**Stage 4 — Report Formatting:** Adds evidence-based data coverage metrics (not fabricated LLM "confidence"), equity disclosures, limitation statements, and human-in-the-loop confirmation for action tools.

---

## The Weibull Survival Model


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



Most civic tech apps sort by date or severity. CivicLens uses **Weibull survival analysis** — the same math used in reliability engineering to predict machine failures.

Every issue gets a **priority score (0–400)** from six components: severity (0–160), Weibull age decay (0–80), school proximity (0–60, max within 200 ft), traffic volume (0–40), weather risk (0–30, freeze-thaw season peaks), and type modifier (0–30). The Weibull CDF models non-linear urgency — a 90-day pothole is 3× more urgent than a 30-day one because the failure probability curve steepens.

Beyond scoring, the model powers **predictive forecasting** (severity at 30/90/180 days, expected failure date) and **cost-of-inaction analysis** (escalating repair costs, daily liability exposure, savings-if-repaired-now) — giving budget analysts concrete numbers instead of vague priorities.

---

## 16 MCP Tools via JSON-RPC 2.0

The MCP server provides **8 read tools** (potholes, sidewalks, schools, work orders, service requests, request status, Chicago 311 benchmarks, data provenance), **4 RBAC-gated action tools** (dispatch crew, update status, schedule inspection, submit service request — all persisted with audit logging), and **4 compute tools** (priority scoring, deterioration forecasting, cost of inaction, what-if budget modeling). The same tools serve the ReAct agent, REST API, and future clients.

---

## Security & Offline Resilience

**Security:** 300 req/min rate limiting, circuit breaker for upstream 429s (300s cooldown), input sanitization (HTML/JS stripping), RBAC (public vs supervisor roles), staff PIN auth (SHA-256 + Bearer tokens), CSP + security headers, CORS allowlist, HTTPS enforcement in production.

**Offline degradation ladder:** Full cloud → partial cloud + local ONNX → local-only intent classification + template reports → keyword fallback. No API key required for basic operation.

---

## Eight Frontend Modules

Built on **Material Design 3** with collapsible side nav, mobile bottom nav, dark mode, and Material Symbols:

1. **Chat** — SSE-streamed pipeline visualization with real-time stage progress and trace data
2. **Service Portal** — 12-category wizard with Leaflet.js map pinning, photo upload, and Power Automate  notifications
3. **Interactive Map** — color-coded circle markers, school markers, city boundary polygon, tabbed severity popups
4. **AI Insights** — auto-generated KPI cards, risk gauges, Chart.js visualizations, custom prompt bar
5. **Staff Operations** — full-page triage dashboard with multi-filter search and crew assignment (PIN-gated)
6. **NLP Dashboard** — six template cards with tab-based results (Overview, Breakdown, Chart)
7. **Report Generator** — 5 templates × 5 audiences, customizable sections, SVG charts, sidebar TOC, inline editing, print/PDF
8. **Demo Mode** — 7-step guided tour with auto-advance, progress dots, and play/pause controls

---

## Email Notifications



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


CivicLens sends automated emails on request submission and status changes, cascading through three transports: **Power Automate webhook** → **SMTP via Nodemailer** → **local HTML preview**. Templates are responsive (mobile 320px+) with a visual progress bar, status-specific colors, activity timeline, and deep-link tracking.

---

## Deployment & Persistence

Deploys to **Azure App Service** via `azd up` (Bicep IaC in `infra/`). **Azure Cosmos DB** (serverless) provides optional cloud persistence — auto-creates containers, seeds from JSON on first boot, syncs all mutations, falls back gracefully to JSON-only mode. GitHub Actions CI runs the full test suite on every push.

---

## Data Methodology

CivicLens uses **real municipal reference data**: actual Lake Forest School District 67 schools at verified GPS coordinates, ASTM D6433 severity methodology, RS Means 2024 cost estimates, federal ADA thresholds, Weibull parameters from published infrastructure engineering literature, and Chicago 311 benchmarks from the Open Data Portal. Infrastructure records use representative sample data calibrated against real municipal patterns — the standard approach for civic tech pilots. Every dataset includes machine-readable provenance metadata via the `get_data_provenance` MCP tool.

---

## How GitHub Copilot Built This

Built entirely with **GitHub Copilot Agent Mode** (Claude)

From a 28-item improvement list, Copilot rewrote the data agent from switch/case to a React loop, added conversation memory, implemented security hardening, built predictive forecasting, wrote 14 test suites, and set up CI in one session.

**Key lesson:** Use AI to review your AI. Copilot caught blind spots that manual testing missed, and the project was stronger for it.

---

## Responsible AI

- **No fabricated metrics** — data coverage from verifiable evidence, not LLM hallucination
- **Source transparency** — every claim links to MCP tools and RAG documents via full pipeline trace
- **Equity awareness** — reports disclose that proximity-based prioritization may advantage certain neighborhoods
- **Human oversight** — action tools require explicit confirmation; all actions logged to audit trail
- **Feedback loop** — users can report inaccuracies directly on generated reports

---

## Try It

- **Live Demo**: [civiclens-app.azurewebsites.net](https://civiclens-app.azurewebsites.net)
- **GitHub**: [github.com/JonEricEubanks/CivicLens](https://github.com/JonEricEubanks/CivicLens)

---

*Built for the JavaScript AI Build-a-thon Season 2. Powered by GitHub Models (GPT-4o-mini + Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct), on-device ONNX inference (MobileBERT), the Model Context Protocol, Azure Cosmos DB, and Node.js.*

title: How I Built an Offline AI-900 Study App in a Few Hours Using VS Code and Copilot
content:
## The Problem

It's December 22nd. I'm packing for my Christmas trip to New York.

Between flights and layovers, I've got hours of downtime. Perfect time to study for my **Azure AI-900 certification**.

One problem: airplane WiFi is either non-existent or costs more than my snacks. Most study apps need internet.

So I built my own offline app. In a few hours. Before my flight.

Ambitious? Maybe. But I had **VSCode Copilot**.


## What I Built

Not just flashcards. Something that actually helps you learn.

- 250+ questions covering all AI-900 topics
- Multiple choice support (the real exam has "select all that apply")
- Explanations for why each answer is right or wrong
- Focus on weak areas automatically
- Works 100% offline
- Dark theme for long flights


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


## Stack

- **VS Code** (not Android Studio)

- Kotlin + Jetpack Compose

- Local DB = zero cloud dependency

- Built with **Copilot **in the loop


## How Copilot Changed Everything

Before: hours of Googling and fiddling.

Now: I describe what I want. Copilot handles the boilerplate.

Me: “Support multiple correct answers.”

Copilot: Updates data model, UI, and validation in one go.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## What Copilot Helped Me Build

- Shuffle questions without repetition

- Show **explanations per option**

- Add animations and polish

- **Track performance** across sessions

- Update the database seamlessly



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## The Result

By the time I finished packing, I had a working app on my phone.


### Quiz Modes:
- Quick, Full, Review, Weak Areas


### Category Filters: 

- CV, GenAI, Conversational AI, etc.


### Smart Feedback: 

- Instant explanations, weak area tracking


### TTS: 

- Listen mode for passive review


## Lessons

Context matters.
The more Copilot understood my codebase, the better its suggestions got.

Describe intent, not implementation.
"Support multiple correct answers" worked better than "add a Boolean field."

Move fast, fix as you go.
Copilot helped me debug issues in real time instead of spending hours stuck.

Offline-first forces good decisions.
Everything works without internet. That's just better architecture.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


## The Hardest Part

Writing 250 quality questions with detailed explanations for every answer option.

That took research and attention. The code was the easy part.


## The Core Takeaway
Copilot didn’t build the app for me. It removed friction so I could focus on learning design, content, and UX.

If you’re not using Copilot for mobile development, you’re wasting time.

title: What I Learned From My First Microsoft MVP Session
excerpt: Understanding the MVP Program I joined a session led by three experienced voices in the Microsoft...
content:
## Understanding the MVP Program


I joined a session led by three experienced voices in the Microsoft community:
[Shrushti Shah (MVP – M365 Copilot), Bhushan Gawale (MVP – Azure AI Foundry), and Alice Piras (Senior Engagement Lead for the MVP Program)](https://youtu.be/AdBENGTBm3o?t=6).

They clarified an important point: the MVP award is not a certification and not something you “apply” for.
It is recognition given to people who already demonstrate consistent, high-quality technical leadership in the Microsoft ecosystem.

MVPs share their expertise they don’t chase the title.



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## How the MVP Process Works

- You cannot nominate yourself. A Microsoft employee or MVP must nominate you.

- You need 12 months of contributions (blogs, talks, GitHub work, mentoring, open-source, etc.).

- Review takes up to 90 days. Rejection is common and normal.

- Content doesn’t have to be in English. Impact matters more than language.

- You must pick one award category (Power Platform, M365, Azure AI, etc.).



![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)



## What MVPs Actually Do


Recognition comes from sustained impact, not random posts or AI-generated content. Examples include:

- Publishing useful blogs and tutorials

- Speaking at meetups and conferences

- Contributing to open-source

- Helping others solve real problems

- Giving Microsoft product feedback

- Mentoring and supporting the community

It’s quality and consistency not volume.


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


## How to Start the MVP Journey


You don’t need to match anyone else’s pace. Focus on steady, meaningful work.

- Turn daily problems you solve into content.

- Choose a contribution style you can sustain.

- Build credibility through clear, helpful explanations.

Protect your energy this should not burn you out.


![Screenshot](data:image/png;base64,)


## The Core Mindset


“You don’t become an MVP by trying to be one. You become one by helping people.”

That’s the difference between burnout and real leadership.
